item.title: Claude Code hooks for path mangling on Windows: an AI fix for an AI problem
item.description:
When I started using Claude Code on Windows, it kept making the same handful of mistakes. It ran python3 and the Microsoft Store opened. It wrote > nul and I ended up with a file called nul that Explorer couldn’t delete. It used /mnt/c/ paths as if it was running in WSL. So I did what you did in the early days of agentic AI: I had Claude vibe code a set of hooks to catch them. An AI fix for an AI problem.

Those hooks turned out to be far more useful than a quick fix usually is: they still rewrite almost half of all Bash commands Claude runs. But Claude got better, and since I wrote them in February the hooks never got a second look. So I went through the three months of logs I had to see which fixes still earn their keep and which now get in the way. Adding the tests the project never had turned up real bugs, including one that silently corrupted every rewritten command containing non-ASCII text. And they showed the real flaw: the hooks could not tell a command from text about a command. That is what v2 fixes.

item.title: Video freezes after a few frames in both Chrome and Firefox: a troubleshooting post-mortem
item.description:
Intermittently, video playback would hang on my Dell XPS 16 9640 laptop. Videos didn’t play at all, or they played a few frames and then froze at 0:00. First I restarted Firefox, but that didn’t help. So I tried the same video in Chrome, and that had exactly the same issue. A reboot did fix it (“reboot immer gut!”), but when you have, like me, lots of tabs and a few Claude Code sessions open, that is really annoying. After it had happened a few times I wanted to know why it was failing.

It looked like a DRM problem. I had recently been tinkering with my provider’s IPTV app and set-top box, because I was interested in how Widevine works, and I had seen that interfering with the DRM halts the video in much the same way. And as described below, this laptop has a few known weak spots for protected video. So that is where I started.

It wasn’t DRM, and it wasn’t the GPU either. This post is a post-mortem of the troubleshooting: what I checked, which tests were misleading and what the real cause turned out to be. Every wrong turn came from the same symptom, and that symptom might fool you too. At the end there is a fix that doesn’t need a reboot, and a small probe tool I wrote to diagnose the problem the next time it happens.

item.title: Default User Profile: Remko’s solution
item.description:
If you are implementing a Citrix, Terminal Server or even just a plain Client-Server environment you will need to create a Default User Profile at some point.

The Default User Profile can be thought of as the initial registry settings that are used when a new profile is created.

Many people think that the Default User Profile is available in regedit via HKEY_USERS.Default but this is NOT the Default User Profile.

item.title: Delphi and Terminal Server Aware
item.description: When an application is not Terminal Server aware (also known as a legacy application), Terminal Server makes certain modifications to the legacy application to make it work properly in a multiuser environment. For example, Terminal Server will create a virtual Windows folder, such that each user gets a Windows folder instead of getting the system’s Windows directory. This gives users access to their own INI files. In addition, Terminal Server makes some adjustments to the registry for a legacy application. These modifications slow the loading of the legacy application on Terminal Server and require up to 8 MegaBytes extra memory. This behaviour can be avoided if the TSAware flag is present in the PE header of an executable as can be read here at MSDN.
